standfirst: A 939-year-old man who cannot die, a woman who was born to end him, and a grim reaper who forgot his own name. What made it hurt was never the fantasy rules. It was the arithmetic: one person ages, the other does not, and the show refuses to pretend that is fine. These six sit with that arithmetic.

picks.why: The closest structural match in the genre. An immortal tethered to a place by an old debt, a mortal who walks in and starts costing her something, and a supporting cast of the dead who each get one perfect episode. Same lush production, same bittersweet contract honoured at the end. Difference: grief-comedy rather than fate-comedy, and the female lead drives everything.

Korean folklore played straight, a centuries-old being in a modern city, and a love that keeps getting reincarnated into worse circumstances. Faster and pulpier than Goblin, with a brother rivalry that is the best thing in it. Difference: it pays a lower emotional price. The sacrifice happens and then the show finds a way around it.

If the part you loved was the world: sworn fates, a magic system with actual rules, and an ensemble that turns into a family. The Hong sisters write comedy into every scene the mythology will allow. Difference: twenty episodes across two parts, and part one ends on a cliff that will annoy you if you stop there.

Kim Eun-sook again, and the one to watch if what got you was the imagery and the doomed grandeur rather than the fantasy. Every frame is composed, every love is on a clock. Difference: no supernatural escape hatch, and the ending is unambiguously tragic.

The same premise with the immortality relocated to another planet: he has waited centuries, she has one lifetime, and the comedy is what keeps it bearable. Difference: much sillier by design, and it resolves the impossible gap with a shrug rather than a cost.

Goblin is secretly a show about what a death leaves behind in a room. This is that thread with the fantasy stripped out entirely: two people clearing the homes of the newly dead. Ten episodes, no romance, and the single cleanest hit of that specific ache. Difference: no fantasy, no comic ensemble and no sweep. It is documentary-plain where Goblin is operatic.

against.title: Descendants of the Sun
against.why: Same writer, same gloss, so it gets paired constantly. But it is a workplace romance in a disaster zone. Nothing is fated, nothing is owed, and the mythology that made Goblin ache is simply absent.

against.title: The King: Eternal Monarch
against.why: The obvious pick: Kim Eun-sook plus a fantasy premise. It is also the one that fails at the only thing that matters here, because the emotional logic never clicks the way the fate logic does.

against.title: Crash Landing on You
against.why: The other great tragic-obstacle romance, in name only. The obstacle there is a border and a bureaucracy, which can be negotiated. Goblin's obstacle is time, which cannot. Different genre of hopelessness.
